title: Water insecurity converts unequal infrastructure and governance into gendered time, safety, health, and livelihood costs
source_unit: UN World Water Development Report 2026: Water for All People – Equal Rights and Opportunities
geography: Global water, sanitation, hygiene, water governance, and water-sector workforce systems

observations.period: 2026 report; global drinking-water access and household water-collection burden

denominator.unit: approximate global population reference for contextualizing water-access estimates

people_without_safely_managed_drinking_w.unit: people lacking safely managed drinking water

daily_water_collection_hours.unit: hours per day women and girls spend collecting water globally, estimated

rural_collection_responsibility.unit: percent-plus of rural households without direct water access in which women are responsible for collection

downstream_costs.value: Unequal water and sanitation access affects health, education, livelihoods, safety, food security, and opportunities for productive and social activity

observations.method: The UN World Water Development Report synthesizes global SDG 6 monitoring, water and sanitation statistics, gender-disaggregated evidence, sector analysis, and policy and governance case material.
observations.uncertainty: Global access estimates and time burdens combine different definitions, survey sources, and local conditions. A reported collection burden does not measure every household's experience, water quality, safety, or the full opportunity cost of time.
observations.subgroup: Women and girls, rural households without direct water access, children, low-income and climate-vulnerable communities, people using water and sanitation services, and households managing water collection and care.
observations.counterinterpretation: Water access has improved in many places, and shared collection, infrastructure, community management, and safer services can reduce burdens. Women’s involvement in water management can also provide valuable local knowledge; the constraint is unequal burden and unequal decision power, not participation itself.

observations.period: 2026 report; water-sector governance and workforce participation

denominator.unit: water-sector workforce percentage reference for reported formal-utility gender representation

women_formal_water_utility_workers.unit: less than percent of formal workers in water utilities worldwide who are women

governance_gap.value: Women are underrepresented in water governance, leadership, financing, technical roles, and infrastructure decision-making

climate_and_disaster_route.value: Climate change, water scarcity, floods, droughts, and disasters intensify existing access and gender inequalities

recommended_response.value: Inclusive water governance, gender-responsive policies, sex-disaggregated data, and sustainable water infrastructure are identified as response routes

observations.method: The report links water access and use to governance, workforce, finance, infrastructure, climate risk, disaster management, and gender-responsive monitoring.
observations.uncertainty: The workforce share is a global summary and does not measure pay, authority, occupational segregation, informal water work, or representation in every country or utility. Policy recommendations are not causal evaluations.
observations.subgroup: Women water-utility workers, community water managers, rural and urban users, infrastructure providers, public agencies, private firms, climate-exposed populations, and decision-makers.
observations.counterinterpretation: More women in water leadership may improve representativeness and system knowledge but cannot substitute for infrastructure finance, reliable operations, or broader accountability. Gender-responsive governance can coexist with difficult distributional tradeoffs over scarce water.

boundary: This record adds a global water-access, gendered-time, governance, workforce, climate, and infrastructure route. It is not respondent-level time-use data, does not estimate individual health or education effects, and does not establish that water access or representation caused any specific household, migration, or political outcome.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: UN-Water and UNESCO official 2026 report summaries and executive-summary materials retrieved; drinking-water gap, water-collection time, rural responsibility, workforce representation, governance, and climate mechanisms cross-checked. Direct local capture was restricted, so the digest records the retrieved evidence summary rather than a claimed local PDF hash.
